title: The Stolen Silver Anklets of the Dancer (ZH)
summary: A pair of musical silver anklets vanishes from a dancer's dressing room. Birbal uses scented oil to catch the culprit among forty palace servants.
full_text:
An accomplished court dancer named Roopa was performing at an imperial festival in Agra when her prized silver ghungroos (musical anklets)—hand-crafted with one hundred silver bells tuned to melodic notes—vanished from her dressing room table during the interval.

Forty maidservants, dressmakers, and stage attendants had been present in the backstage corridors. Every single woman denied seeing the anklets, weeping and protesting her innocence.

Akbar summoned Birbal to find the heirloom bells before the festival concluded.

Birbal had all forty attendants brought into a darkened anteroom. In the center of the room sat a large bronze cauldron filled with water, heavily scented with fragrant sandalwood and rose oil.

Birbal announced to the women:

'Inside this cauldron rests an enchanted silver fish gifted by an Arabian mystic. Each of you must step forward in the dark, plunge both hands deep into the water, and pull them out.

'When an innocent woman dips her hands, the fish remains calm. But when the thief dips her hands, the silver bells of the anklet will chime from within the cauldron, marking her for the guards!'

One by one, the forty women walked to the cauldron in the dark, plunged their hands into the water, and stepped back. Not a chime was heard.

Birbal then ordered torches brought into the room.

'Now,' Birbal said with a gentle smile, 'hold your hands up to your faces, and let the Emperor smell your palms!'

Thirty-nine women held out hands that were dripping with water and heavily scented with the rich, sweet fragrance of sandalwood and rose oil.

However, one maidservant held out hands that were completely dry and scentless!

Birbal pointed to her: 'Here is your thief!'

'How can you know?' Akbar asked.

Birbal explained:

'Sire, the story of the magic silver fish was a complete invention. Thirty-nine innocent women trusted their clear conscience, reached deep into the cauldron, and soaked their hands in the scented water.

'But the thief, terrified that the magic bells would chime in the cauldron, merely hovered her dry hands near the rim without touching the water at all!'

Caught red-handed by her dry palms, the trembling maid confessed, pulled the silver anklets from inside her apron, and returned them to the joyful dancer. Akbar praised Birbal's psychological genius.
